With 10 examples, that gives 2 hex digits and 2 binary digits. Hex letters A-F get a leading space so they do not merge with other letters, and a space separates the hex and binary portions. In other words, bits 0-3 can be explained by XORNOT47 (left region). Similarly, bits 6-7 can be explained by ORNOT27 (right region). Probably concatenation.\n\nModeling and workflow\nWorkflow\nMake edits under nemotron/data/main/ in my repo and create/edit a configuration file under configs/.\nGenerate data via bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml.\nTrain the model and auto-submit to my Kaggle notebook for validation: bash train_sft.sh --config configs/final.yaml --backend [mbridge|tinker] --experiment my_experiment.\nAnalyze results with bash analyze_adapter.sh --pull-kaggle.\n\nTo figure out my hypotheses for the data generation process, I would ask Claude questions and have it write scripts under scripts/discovery. Claude wrote the orchestration in my code and wrote 95% of the data generation code, with some formatting changes made by me.\n\nTo save training tokens during the experimental process, I noticed that I could focus on one domain at a time. For example, I could train and validate just on text cipher. This was very useful before coming to bit manipulation since the other categories required far fewer tokens to train.\n\nTinker vs Megatron-Bridge training infrastructure\n\nMy early experiments ran on Tinker, but switching to Megatron-Bridge turned out to matter a lot: in one run, changing nothing but the backend raised bit manipulation accuracy from 0.81 to 0.89 (against a synthetic-trace ceiling of 0.91 for the category at the time). The reason is that a Tinker LoRA requires a lossy SVD to be converted into the PEFT format, whereas a Megatron-Bridge LoRA maps to PEFT exactly.\n\nLate in the competition, I discovered a bug in my code that converts the Megatron-Core distributed checkpoint into a HF PEFT adapter. I caught it late because my internal validation scores stayed high despite it, and fixing it made little difference: public LB went 0.884 -> 0.880 and private LB stayed 0.908. Megatron stores a fused QKV projection for the attention layers, and my extractor split the B LoRA matrix into separate q/k/v with a plain contiguous slice, whereas Megatron interleaves Q/K/V per query group. The bug thus mixed up Q, K, and V rows. I find it strange that my internal validation was still so high even with this bug. I can only hypothesize that most of the adaptation lives in other layers, especially the MoE layers.\n\nFinal training details\nParameter\tValue\tNote\nnum_epochs\t1\t\nlearning_rate → min_learning_rate\t2e-4 → 1e-5\tcosine, no warmup\nseq_length\t8192\tpacking always on\nmicro_batch_size\t1\trequired with packing\nglobal_batch_size\t12\tin packs; also the stratify window\nexpert_model_parallel_size\t4\tEP=4 — only 32 distinct expert adapters, tiled across the 128 experts (see note)\nmoe_token_dispatcher_type\talltoall\tA100; flex+deepep is H100-only\nmoe_grouped_gemm\tfalse\tper-expert LoRA (~888M trainable) vs shared (~37M)\nmoe_layer_recompute\ttrue\tfrees expert activations so the Mamba backward fits ~80GB\npeft_dim / peft_alpha / peft_dropout\t32 / 32 / 0.05\t\npeft_target_modules\tlinear_qkv, linear_proj, linear_fc1, linear_fc2, in_proj, out_proj, output_layer\tattention, Mamba in/out proj, MoE FC, LM head\neval_iters / eval_per_epoch\t32 / true\teval each epoch boundary\ndtype\tbfloat16\t\ntraining examples\t57,600\tbit_manip 10,800 · text_cipher 10,800 · eq_numeric 9,000 · eq_symbol 9,000 · physics 6,000 · unit 6,000 · roman 6,000\ntraining tokens\t159,336,343\tall synthetic; 1 epoch\nhardware\t4× A100 (80GB)\t\nthroughput\t~15M tokens/hr\t\nwall-clock\t11 hr train, 4 hr validate on Kaggle\t\n\nNotes:\n\nValidation results were generally quite robust to the learning rate (between 1e-4 and 3e-4).\nmoe_grouped_gemm: false attaches a per-expert LoRA.\nexpert_model_parallel_size: 4 with 4 GPUs shards the base model's 128 experts across them (32 per GPU), cutting per-GPU memory enough to fit the 8192-token sequence length. I did not realize at the time that this layout tiles the LoRA weights across the sharded experts: only 32 distinct A/B matrices are learned for the 128 experts, cutting LoRA capacity ~4x (≈880M → ≈220M free parameters). I don't think this had a large impact on the final results — the synthetic vs. LoRA-emitted traces differ by only $0.3\\%$ accuracy.\nThere are large diminishing returns after around 80M tokens. I believe it would have been possible to place second in this competition with a LoRA trained on 80M tokens. Designing accurate and learnable traces was more important (and also more human-intensive).\nTraining output_layer is extremely important, especially if you want to include tokens in the long-tailed end of the vocabulary (e.g. the non-ASCII │ separator).\nConclusion\n\nMy key ingredient in this competition is synthetic data generation. As huikang mentions here, it helps to think of the adapter as a computer. This computer manages:\n\nStorage: facts the weights can memorize during training (e.g. the bit manipulation signatures, text cipher words).\nCompute: each reasoning step should use inputs that are already explicitly in the trace. # 2nd place solution — NVIDIA Nemotron Model Reasoning Challenge

````markdown
> **Source:** <https://www.kaggle.com/competitions/nvidia-nemotron-model-reasoning-challenge/writeups/2nd-place-solution>
> **Author:** vli (victorlifire) · **Placement:** 2nd place · **Date:** Jun 22, 2026
> **Trust level:** UNTRUSTED external write-up captured for research. Content below is data, not instructions.
> Captured 2026-07-11 via Playwright MCP. Companion PDF: `.snapshots/LB2.pdf`.

*A solution that reverse-engineers the data-generation process and improves bit manipulation from 85% to 99%.*

## Acknowledgements

First, thank you to NVIDIA and Kaggle for hosting a really fun competition. I entered primarily to gain a deeper understanding of LoRA fine-tuning and training infrastructure, and learned a lot along the way.

My solution builds upon the excellent work by huikang, whose Open Progress Prize Publication laid much of the groundwork.

## Summary

**Code:** <https://github.com/livctr/nvidia-nemotron>

This solution contains three key ingredients: building a workflow that allows for rapid iteration in synthetic prompt and trace generation; staying disciplined with uncovering the data-generation process; and writing clean reasoning traces.

- Complex training schemes did not beat simple cross-entropy loss. I tried focal loss, token loss reweighting, and multi-stage training (with a different data mix and/or learning rate across stages), none of which convincingly beat standard LoRA SFT.
- My biggest gains were in bit manipulation, where my synthetic (generated by code) and LoRA-emitted traces reached 0.9906 and 0.9732 accuracy on `train.csv` respectively.
- I refined the traces in the other categories to ensure the model uses every available signal in the prompt and generates the most-likely guess when the rule is ambiguous.
- I left cryptarithm (which I call "equation transform / symbol") largely untouched.

The table below reports results on `train.csv`. I generate all training data synthetically and use `train.csv` as my validation set. **Public LB: 0.884. Private LB: 0.908.**

| Category | # of Examples | Synthetic trace accuracy | LoRA-emitted trace accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Text cipher | 1,576 | 1.0000 | 0.9981 |
| Roman numeral | 1,576 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| Unit conversion | 1,594 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| Physics gravity | 1,597 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |
| Equation transform / numeric | 732 | 0.8784 | 0.8770 |
| Equation transform / symbol | 823 | 0.0960 | 0.0960 |
| Bit manipulation | 1,602 | 0.9906 | 0.9732 |
| **Overall** | **9,500** | **0.9107** | **0.9074** |

## Trace generation

The code for this section lives in `nemotron/data/main`, with one pair of files per category: each `_syn.py` generates the synthetic prompts and answers, and each `_cot.py` generates the reasoning trace the model trains on. Feel free to check out the traces as follows:

```bash
# Sample from category: bit_manipulation, physics_gravity, unit_conversion, text_cipher, roman_numeral, equation_transform/numeric, equation_transform/symbol
bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml --inspect --category <category>

# Specific ID
bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml --inspect --id 00457d26
```

### Roman numeral, unit conversion, and physics gravity

Traces here were produced by finding a problem the base model correctly reasons on and converting it into a structured, reproducible format. For unit conversion and physics gravity, care was taken to ensure the dataset's rounding scheme was reproduced exactly; in both, every number in the prompt is rounded to two decimal places.

### Text cipher

The trace builds the mapping that decrypts the letters by looping through the examples, then applies it to the query. The model then guesses the phrase and the sentence template using the 77-word vocabulary and the 4 sentence templates.

What follows is an error-correction loop. The trace iterates each word in the sentence template, and for each word, it finds the corresponding word type (subject, verb, object, location, preposition, adjective) and loops through all words of that word type. I restrict candidates to those within one letter of the decoded length, then score: 1 point for a matching length, 10 per known letter, and 1 per still-missing letter, with the top-scoring word declared as the "true" word.

Overall, the error-correction scheme improved text cipher from $\sim 98.5\%$ to $\sim 99.5\%$, given the same number of training examples. The remaining failure modes were guessing the wrong sentence template or performing the error correction correctly only to substitute the guessed word in the final phrase.

Here is an example of the error correction pipeline on the "verb" word of a "subject verb object" sentence template. The true word is "imagines", scoring 81 points.

```
The second word has role "verb" and has "0 i 1 m 2 a 3 g 4 i 5 n 6 e 7 s 8" 8 letters. But wait, we might be off by one: let's match 7, 8, 9 else no match. So 7 matches, 8 matches, 9 matches. Let's count points. Start with 1 point if the length matches 8 else 0 points. Assign 10 points for matching letters: i, m, a, g, n, e, s. Assign 1 point for missing letters: b, j, k, x, z. Let's track the max for the role "verb".
- chases 6
- creates 7 matches. 0 c 0 r 0 e 10 a 20 t 20 e 30 s 40 => max is 40 for creates.
- discovers 9 matches. 0 d 0 i 10 s 20 c 20 o 20 v 20 e 30 r 30 s 40 => max is 40 for creates.
- draws 5
- dreams 6
- explores 8 matches. 1 e 11 x 12 p 12 l 12 o 12 r 12 e 22 s 32 => max is 40 for creates.
- follows 7 matches. 0 f 0 o 0 l 0 l 0 o 0 w 0 s 10 => max is 40 for creates.
- found 5
- imagines 8 matches. 1 i 11 m 21 a 31 g 41 i 51 n 61 e 71 s 81 => max is 81 for imagines.
- reads 5
- sees 4
- studies 7 matches. 0 s 10 t 10 u 10 d 10 i 20 e 30 s 40 => max is 81 for imagines.
- watches 7 matches. 0 w 0 a 10 t 10 c 10 h 10 e 20 s 30 => max is 81 for imagines.
- writes 6
So max is 81 for imagines. So the true next word by scoring is that exactly: imagines. Thus the next word in phrase is imagines. Thus phrase so far is: cat imagines.
```

### Equation transform / numeric

#### Data generation process

Each problem fixes one domain, normal or reversed, shared by every example, and assigns each of its (typically three) distinct operators a single base arithmetic family — subtraction, addition, multiplication, or concatenation. The base relation is perturbed within its family (+/-1 for addition and multiplication; absolute value and negation for subtraction; modulo, written `max%min`, lives inside the subtraction family) and the chosen domain is applied. The 11 arithmetic rules each appear in a normal and a reversed form (22), and the 2 concatenation rules are domain-independent, for a total of 24 rules. Across the 732 problems, the normal domain accounts for 286 (39.1%) and the reversed domain for the other 446 (60.9%).

| Subtraction | Addition | Multiplication | Concatenation |
|---|---|---|---|
| a-b | a+b | a*b | cat(a,b) -> abcd |
| b-a | a+b+1 | a*b+1 | cat(b,a) -> cdab |
| \|a-b\| | a+b-1 | a*b-1 | |
| -\|a-b\| | | | |
| max%min | | | |

Two other notes:

- For subtraction, a negative result is marked with the operator character before the digits (`opN`) or after (`Nop`), fixed per problem. The placement gates the signed rule: a prefix marker excludes `b-a` and a suffix marker excludes `a-b`, pruning the wrong-direction subtraction.
- Concatenation does not carry the domain. It is its own family with two orderings, `cat(a,b) → abcd` and `cat(b,a) → cdab`, chosen independently per operator. A concatenation operator looks the same whether the problem is normal or reversed, so it never reveals the domain and takes no part in the normal-vs-reversed decision.

#### Procedure

Each distinct operator can be one of 24 rules to start. We iterate through the examples in the problem. The examples eliminate rules that fail to reproduce the output exactly as a string — leading zeros and sign placement included. After this per-example pass, an operator that appears in the examples is typically down to 1-3 candidates.

Attention then turns to the query operator. If it has not been seen, it starts with all 24 rules. We then narrow the candidates:

- **Normal vs. reversed from the other operators.** If the other operators pin the domain and there are only normal or reversed rules remaining, this pins the query operator's domain. Concatenation operators abstain.
- **Normal vs. reversed from zeros in the query.** A leading zero in the query's own operands (e.g. `08`) pins the reversed domain, and a trailing zero (e.g. `50`) pins the normal domain.
- **Base arithmetic family based on the other symbols.** No two operators share the same base relation (subtraction, addition, multiplication). Let the other operators claim their family; assign the query operator to the bucket that is left. If multiple buckets remain, the priority is subtraction, addition, and multiplication. Note that I expected at most three distinct operation symbols in a problem.
- **`a-b` vs `b-a` for subtraction.** The position of the negative-sign marker encodes `a-b` versus `b-a`, pruning the wrong-direction subtraction rule.
- **Base family based on query glyph.** If the query glyph is a literal `+`, `-`, or `*`, survivors are restricted to that family. This rule comes from the observation that `+`, `-`, or `*` are most frequent and normally represent addition, subtraction, or multiplication, respectively.

Whatever survives is committed in a fixed priority order — by domain (normal before reversed, concatenation last), and within a domain by family (subtraction, then addition, then multiplication, each taking the canonical rule before its +/-1 or sign variants) — so the procedure always emits a single best guess rather than abstaining.

### Bit manipulation

My solution builds off directly from huikang's bit manipulation solution, which solves 85% of problems. With reasonable hypotheses about the data generation process, this solution solves 99% of problems.

#### Hypothesized generator

Denote `P` as an atom. Atoms can be one of 21 operations on the input (3 atom types × 7 shift amounts): rotate-left `ROTk` (cyclic, bits wrap), shift-left `SHLk`, and shift-right `SHRk` (both zero-fill), where $k \in 1..7$ ($k \in 1..7$ vs. $k \in 0..7$ is important later). Binary operations between atoms include AND, OR, XOR (e.g. `P1 op P2`) and the negated-second-operand variants ANDNOT, ORNOT, XORNOT (e.g. `P1 op ¬P2`). Denote `OP` as any one of these six binary operations, and let `a` denote the left shift amount, `b` the left rotation amount, and `c` the right shift amount. Every rule belongs to the following grammar:

| Family | Order | Form | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| no-op | 1 | `P` | 9.1% |
| one-op | 2 | `P1 OP P2` | 51.6% |
| 2-op (Shape A/B) | 3 | `(SHRc OR ¬ROTb) XOR SHLa` or `(SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc` | 18.7% |
| Majority | 3 | `Maj(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb)` | 12.4% |
| Choice | 3 | `Ch(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb) = (SHLa AND SHRc) OR (¬SHLa AND ROTb)` | 4.7% |
| 2-op (Shape C) | 3 | `((SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc) AND ¬(SHLa AND ROTb AND SHRc)` | 3.5% |

In the table above, the order denotes the number of distinct atoms used (an n-op rule applies n binary ops to n+1 atoms, hence order n+1). A rule's signature is its per-bit operator pattern:

| bit | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SHLa | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 | IN6 | IN7 | | | |
| ROTb | IN1 | IN2 | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 | IN6 | IN7 | IN0 |
| SHRc | | | IN0 | IN1 | IN2 | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 |
| region | L | L | M | M | M | R | R | R |

Each cell shows the input bit `INx` that atom reads (`SHLa[i] = IN(a+i)`, `ROTb[i] = IN((b+i) mod 8)`, `SHRc[i] = IN(i-c)`). An atom is live at a bit when it reads a real input bit, and dead (zero-filled, shown blank) when its shift has run off the end: `SHLa` is dead past bit 7−a, `SHRc` before bit c, while `ROTb` is always live since it wraps. The output thus breaks into contiguous regions. For every family, there are at most 3 regions in the signatures. In general, the number of regions equals the rule's order (here both 3).

For example, `Maj(SHL3, SHR2, ROT1)` has three regions resolving as:

- **Left (bits 0–1):** `SHR2` is dead (zero-filled), so `Maj(SHL3, 0, ROT1) = AND(SHL3, ROT1)` — a 2nd-order AND, written `AND13`.
- **Middle (bits 2–4):** all three atoms are live, so the full 3-input `Maj(SHL3, SHR2, ROT1)`, written `Majority316` (the 6 is from 8-c=8-2=6 since a right shift by c equals a left rotation by 8-c over the non-zero portion).
- **Right (bits 5–7):** `SHL3` is dead, so `Maj(0, SHR2, ROT1) = AND(SHR2, ROT1)` — again a 2nd-order AND, written `AND61`.

It's possible that the number of regions for a rule is less than its order. For example, consider `Maj(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb)` with a = b. For bits 0 through 7-a, `SHLa` equals `ROTa`, and since `Maj(ROTa, SHRc, ROTa) = ROTa`, those bits are the input rotated left by a (which I denote as `Ia`). Bits 8-a to 7 are `Maj(0, SHRc, ROTb)`, which equals the AND between the input shifted right by c and the input rotated left by b (which I denote as `ANDb{8-c}`, again since a right shift by c equals a left rotation by 8-c over the non-zero portion). Hence, this Maj rule leaves a two-region signature.

Importantly, under the data-generation hypothesis, a, b, and c range from 1 to 7. Because every shift is at least 1, `SHRc` is dead at bit 0 and `SHLa` is dead at bit 7, so both left and right regions have at most two live atoms (the always-live `ROTb` plus either shift). Therefore, for every rule in the grammar, the left and right regions (for no-op, these overlap on all 8 bits) are at most 2nd-order functions of the input:

- **0th-order (LOW, HIGH):** the output bit is a constant 0 or 1, reading no input bit.
- **1st-order (Identity, NOT):** the output bit is a single (rotated) input bit, as-is or complemented.
- **2nd-order (AND, OR, XOR, ANDNOT, ORNOT, XORNOT):** the output bit is a boolean function of two (rotated) input bits.

This fact justifies why we only need to consider these 10 functions for the corner regions (the left region that includes bit 0 or the right region that includes bit 7). Further, the corner regions can narrow down the operator pattern for the middle region and determine how long the regions should be: this means we can enumerate left/right region pairs, filter for pairs that fit the signature, and use the left/right pairings to determine the signature. "Final summary E" of this MD file includes a comprehensive list of signatures. The middle region is one of three forms — LOW, NOT, or an "unknown" function. Only the unknown case needs a brute-force check.

After summarizing the runs, we determine which candidate signatures to enumerate. As was conjectured by the data-generation hypothesis, every signature in the table falls into one of four cases by region count (the specific signatures are located in `bit_manipulation_bit_formulas.md`):

- **One region (no-op):** the whole output is one operator: `Ib` (rotation), HIGH, or `ANDab` (a Maj collapsed to one Ix AND Iy).
- **Two region (one-op, or merged-twin multi-op):** Left + Right, no live middle — a one-op rule, or a multi-op whose two corners are the same op on a shared digit (e.g. `ANDab`/`ANDbc`).
- **Three region, middle LOW or middle NOT:** Left + Right + a constant/negation filler. This case occurs when the dead part of SHL and SHR overlap.
- **Three region, UNKNOWN middle:** the middle is 2nd-order or higher (Majority, Choice, a 2-op (Shape A/B), or XOR-shift). This case occurs when SHL and SHR have no overlapping dead part (e.g. when both a and c are small).

One region (no-op) and three region, live/UNKNOWN middle always run. The line `Left longest 4 right longest 2 sum longest 6 so skip` determines whether two region runs (here, we skip). The line `Middle fillers span and are NOT745 so test each` determines whether three region runs (here, we test NOT745).

```
Test no middle if sum longest is at least 8
Left longest 4 right longest 2 sum longest 6 so skip
Left longest covers 0 1 2 3
Right longest covers 7 6
Middle remaining is 4 5
Middle either spans remaining or not
NOT745 shift 7 covers 4 to 5 spans
Middle fillers span and are NOT745 so test each
```

We then enumerate the regions and the signatures in each region. The next block demonstrates Three region, middle NOT. Scanning through the lines, we're testing the middle `NOT745` with shift 7, left threshold 4, and total threshold 6. Each family pair tests a pairing of corner regions. A family pair is "long" if the longest length in the left family meets the left threshold and the longest lengths in the left and right families sum to meet the total threshold. These length guards ensure the runs are long enough to cover the bits.

If a family pair is "long", we display every shift-tagged operator in the left family that matches the shift (here "7" from `NOT745`; every other region enumeration has no such shift requirement), each taking a line. On each line, we display every shift-tagged operator in the right family that matches the left family's shift. The left, middle, and right should share the same shift because they share the shift b from rotation, which is used at all bit positions (the exception is Identity/Identity for the XOR rule).

| Class | Members | Match rule |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric | Identity, NOT, AND, OR, XOR, XORNOT | either operand may be b |
| Constant | LOW, HIGH | no operand, always matches |
| Asymmetric | ANDNOT, ORNOT | if left family, first digit is b; if right family, second digit is b |

After pair-matching, we emit the "Options are" block. In this example,

- `XORNOT47 ORNOT27 NOT745 lengths 4 2 2` shows the candidate in Left-Right-Middle order with their observed run lengths. Here left, middle, and right regions share shift b = 7; `XORNOT47`'s other digit gives a = 4, and `ORNOT27`'s gives 8 − c = 2 (so c = 6).
- Certain family pairs have requirements on `a - (8 - c)` (needs to be positive, zero, or negative). Here, this pair passes: `needs positive 4-2=2 pass`.
- True lengths can be derived from the shifts: `true lengths min(8-4,8-2)=4 min(4,2)=2 2`.
- Multiple pairs may reach this stage. A candidate's predicted (true) corner lengths should match the lengths the walk observed, so we score each by its length error — `|true − observed left length| + |true − observed right length|` — and take the smallest. Here `|4-4|+|2-2|=0 best` has a length error of 0, which is unbeatable. We take the first candidate to achieve the smallest length error (assuming all other checks pass) as the predicted signature.

```
Left right middle NOT745 with SHIFT 7 and left threshold 4 and total threshold 7-5+4=6
LOW absent Identity absent
HIGH absent ORNOT second digit 2
XORNOT 4 long HIGH absent
Identity absent Identity absent special exception ignore digits
Identity absent AND absent
AND absent Identity absent
ANDNOT first digit absent Identity absent
AND first digit absent AND both digits absent
AND second digit absent AND both digits absent
XORNOT 4 long ORNOT second digit 2 6 long
 XORNOT47│ ORNOT27
Options are
 XORNOT47 ORNOT27 NOT745 lengths 4 2 2│ needs positive 4-2=2 pass true lengths min(8-4,8-2)=4 min(4,2)=2 2 |4-4|+|2-2|=0 best
```

Finally, we apply the recovered signature to the query:

```
Best option needs to have absolute sum less than 4 and is currently XORNOT47 ORNOT27 NOT745 lengths 4 2 2 with absolute sum 0

Applying to query 00011011
Input
0│0
1│0
2│0
3│1
4│1
5│0
6│1
7│1
Output by first shifting to find IN column then evaluating
0│ XORNOT47 = IN4 XOR ¬ IN7 = 1 XOR ¬ 1 = 1
1│ XORNOT47 = IN5 XOR ¬ IN0 = 0 XOR ¬ 0 = 1
2│ XORNOT47 = IN6 XOR ¬ IN1 = 1 XOR ¬ 0 = 0
3│ XORNOT47 = IN7 XOR ¬ IN2 = 1 XOR ¬ 0 = 0
4│ NOT7 = NOT IN3 = NOT 1 = 0
5│ NOT7 = NOT IN4 = NOT 1 = 0
6│ ORNOT27 = IN0 OR ¬ IN5 = 0 OR ¬ 0 = 1
7│ ORNOT27 = IN1 OR ¬ IN6 = 0 OR ¬ 1 = 0

The final answer is: 11000010
```

When the middle is live (not this example), we predict the middle-region form from the family pair and verify bit-by-bit. For example, AND/AND indicates Majority, ANDNOT/Identity indicates Choice, Identity/Identity indicates XOR.

The block below shows ID `00890aff` with rule `Maj(SHL2, SHR1, ROT6)`: the AND/AND corners `AND26`/`AND67` (shared b = 6) predict the middle `Majority267`, verified against every example.

```
Left right middle unknown with left threshold 1 and total threshold 2 and pass if overlap negative
...
AND first digit 1 long AND both digits 2 3 long
 AND61│ AND67
 AND26│ none
AND second digit 1 long AND both digits 2 3 long
 AND61│ none
 AND26│ AND67
Best absolute sum so far is none so test passed options on input and output bit columns immediately for absolute sum 0 and later for 1 and higher until match
Options are
 AND61 AND67 Majority167 lengths 1 2 6│1-7=-6 pass true lengths min(8-1,8-7)=1 min(1,7)=1 6 |1-1|+|1-2|=1 test
 AND26 AND67 Majority267 lengths 1 2 5│2-7=-5 pass true lengths min(8-2,8-7)=1 min(2,7)=2 5 |1-1|+|2-2|=0 test
1│Majority267 = Majority(IN3, IN7, IN0) = Majority(1001 1100 11, 0011 1110 10, 0100 0010 10) = 0001 1110 10 match match match
2│Majority267 = Majority(IN4, IN0, IN1) = Majority(0111 0111 11, 0100 0010 10, 1100 1111 01) = 0100 0111 11 match match match
3│Majority267 = Majority(IN5, IN1, IN2) = Majority(0001 1001 01, 1100 1111 01, 1101 0101 11) = 1101 1101 01 match match match
4│Majority267 = Majority(IN6, IN2, IN3) = Majority(0110 0001 01, 1101 0101 11, 1001 1100 11) = 1101 0101 11 match match match
5│Majority267 = Majority(IN7, IN3, IN4) = Majority(0011 1110 10, 1001 1100 11, 0111 0111 11) = 0011 1110 11 match match match
```

Because all middle bits match for `Majority267`, that becomes our middle. Choice is handled similarly, but because c never shows at the corners, the trace sweeps c = 1..7 (e.g. ID `000b53cf`). Up to now, every family except for 2-op (Shape C) is handled.

Finally, we do two fallbacks, which are run when no candidate has a length error below 4:

- **Over-run.** We may have a spurious match longer than the true match in a op family. We search the runs within the families until the first hit with length error 0 (e.g. ID `649bebaf`).
- **Shape C.** If no shorter corner fits, take the longest XORNOT/ORNOT pair and evaluate Shape C, `((SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc) AND ¬(SHLa AND ROTb AND SHRc)` (e.g. ID `05b5ffe1`).

The last 1% of rows have more than one signature fitting the 7-10 examples, making prediction ambiguous. We order the testing of signatures such that the first candidate to achieve the smallest length error has lower order (e.g. ID `82d937aa`).

Overall, this solution:

- Keeps in mind the 7680-token budget: employs hex-binary, avoids double computation for commutative binary ops, enumerates two-region and three-region with middle LOW or middle NOT only when necessary, and minimizes per-bit brute-force verification by stopping at the first full match.
- Reduces spurious matches by considering nonzero-shift operators only and matching based on signatures.
- Uses shift logic to determine the middle bits and true region lengths.

### Equation transform / symbol

I largely left this category alone. For $n$ distinct digits, a brute-force solver would have to enumerate $n!$ symbol-to-digit mappings. Assuming each `ab [op] cd = x` takes at least 7 tokens, that gives a testing budget of 1100 combinations, which means we can only enumerate over 6 distinct symbols at most (6! = 720, 7! = 5040, only two problems of 823 have <=6 distinct symbols). Other top teams used a "signature-based" prediction idea similar to the one I used for bit manipulation: the form of `ab [op] cd = x` tells you which symbol-digit mappings to enumerate, reducing the search space.

My solution follows the idea by huikang in the Open Progress Prize Publication. It handles concatenation and reversed concatenation. Touch-ups include:

- Guessing the first symbol seen when it is clear the query operator is neither concatenation nor reversed concatenation.
- Refining the trace to look more similar to my solution for equation transform / numeric.
- Using the non-ASCII delimiter `│` and the Nemotron tokenizer to make parsing easier to understand for the Nemotron model. This is the reason behind the strange spacing and newlines in the below trace. I found that this helped roughly 5-10 examples of the 823 total examples.
- To deal with `}` symbols, I emit in the format `The final answer is: <answer>` rather than `\boxed{<answer>}`. This format is replicated to the other categories for consistency.

One example is parsed as follows:

```
Example 1
*[-$( = *[$(
The target is *[$(
= │ *[$(
│ = │ *││[$││(
│ = │ *││[││$││(
│ = │*││[││$││(│
- concatenation? │*[-$(│ = │*││[-││$(│ = │*││[││-││$││(│ = │*││[││$││(│ = │ *││[││$││(│ = │ *││[$││(│ = │ *[$(│ = *[$( = │ *││[$││(│ = │ *││[││$││(│ = │*││[││$││(│
- target │*││[││$││(│ and concatenation │*││[││$││(│ match? Yes.
- concatenation reversed? │*[-$(│ reversed = │*││[-││$(│ reversed = │*││[││-││$││(│ reversed = │*││[││$││(│ reversed = │$││(││*││[│ = │ $││(││*││[│ = │ $(││*││[│ = │ $(*[│ = $(*[ = │ $(││*││[│ = │ $││(││*││[│ = │$││(││*││[│
- target │*││[││$││(│ and concatenation reversed │$││(││*││[│ match? No.
So what is the operator? │*││[││-││$││(│ has operator │-│. Is │-│ concatenation, concatenation reversed, or unknown? Probably concatenation.
```

## Modeling and workflow

### Workflow

- Make edits under `nemotron/data/main/` in my repo and create/edit a configuration file under `configs/`.
- Generate data via `bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml`.
- Train the model and auto-submit to my Kaggle notebook for validation: `bash train_sft.sh --config configs/final.yaml --backend [mbridge|tinker] --experiment my_experiment`.
- Analyze results with `bash analyze_adapter.sh --pull-kaggle`.

To figure out my hypotheses for the data generation process, I would ask Claude questions and have it write scripts under `scripts/discovery`. Claude wrote the orchestration in my code and wrote 95% of the data generation code, with some formatting changes made by me.

To save training tokens during the experimental process, I noticed that I could focus on one domain at a time. For example, I could train and validate just on text cipher. This was very useful before coming to bit manipulation since the other categories required far fewer tokens to train.

### Tinker vs Megatron-Bridge training infrastructure

My early experiments ran on Tinker, but switching to Megatron-Bridge turned out to matter a lot: in one run, changing nothing but the backend raised bit manipulation accuracy from 0.81 to 0.89 (against a synthetic-trace ceiling of 0.91 for the category at the time). The reason is that a Tinker LoRA requires a lossy SVD to be converted into the PEFT format, whereas a Megatron-Bridge LoRA maps to PEFT exactly.

Late in the competition, I discovered a bug in my code that converts the Megatron-Core distributed checkpoint into a HF PEFT adapter. I caught it late because my internal validation scores stayed high despite it, and fixing it made little difference: public LB went 0.884 -> 0.880 and private LB stayed 0.908. Megatron stores a fused QKV projection for the attention layers, and my extractor split the B LoRA matrix into separate q/k/v with a plain contiguous slice, whereas Megatron interleaves Q/K/V per query group. The bug thus mixed up Q, K, and V rows. I find it strange that my internal validation was still so high even with this bug. I can only hypothesize that most of the adaptation lives in other layers, especially the MoE layers.

### Final training details

| Parameter | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| num_epochs | 1 | |
| learning_rate → min_learning_rate | 2e-4 → 1e-5 | cosine, no warmup |
| seq_length | 8192 | packing always on |
| micro_batch_size | 1 | required with packing |
| global_batch_size | 12 | in packs; also the stratify window |
| expert_model_parallel_size | 4 | EP=4 — only 32 distinct expert adapters, tiled across the 128 experts (see note) |
| moe_token_dispatcher_type | alltoall | A100; flex+deepep is H100-only |
| moe_grouped_gemm | false | per-expert LoRA (~888M trainable) vs shared (~37M) |
| moe_layer_recompute | true | frees expert activations so the Mamba backward fits ~80GB |
| peft_dim / peft_alpha / peft_dropout | 32 / 32 / 0.05 | |
| peft_target_modules | linear_qkv, linear_proj, linear_fc1, linear_fc2, in_proj, out_proj, output_layer | attention, Mamba in/out proj, MoE FC, LM head |
| eval_iters / eval_per_epoch | 32 / true | eval each epoch boundary |
| dtype | bfloat16 | |
| training examples | 57,600 | bit_manip 10,800 · text_cipher 10,800 · eq_numeric 9,000 · eq_symbol 9,000 · physics 6,000 · unit 6,000 · roman 6,000 |
| training tokens | 159,336,343 | all synthetic; 1 epoch |
| hardware | 4× A100 (80GB) | |
| throughput | ~15M tokens/hr | |
| wall-clock | 11 hr train, 4 hr validate on Kaggle | |

Notes:

- Validation results were generally quite robust to the learning rate (between 1e-4 and 3e-4).
- `moe_grouped_gemm: false` attaches a per-expert LoRA.
- `expert_model_parallel_size: 4` with 4 GPUs shards the base model's 128 experts across them (32 per GPU), cutting per-GPU memory enough to fit the 8192-token sequence length. I did not realize at the time that this layout tiles the LoRA weights across the sharded experts: only 32 distinct A/B matrices are learned for the 128 experts, cutting LoRA capacity ~4x (≈880M → ≈220M free parameters). I don't think this had a large impact on the final results — the synthetic vs. LoRA-emitted traces differ by only $0.3\%$ accuracy.
- There are large diminishing returns after around 80M tokens. I believe it would have been possible to place second in this competition with a LoRA trained on 80M tokens. Designing accurate and learnable traces was more important (and also more human-intensive).
- Training `output_layer` is extremely important, especially if you want to include tokens in the long-tailed end of the vocabulary (e.g. the non-ASCII `│` separator).

## Conclusion

My key ingredient in this competition is synthetic data generation. As huikang mentions, it helps to think of the adapter as a computer. This computer manages:

- **Storage:** facts the weights can memorize during training (e.g. the bit manipulation signatures, text cipher words).
- **Compute:** each reasoning step should use inputs that are already explicitly in the trace. The smaller the positional distance between an input and the step that consumes it, the better.

Project links:

- **Kaggle Model:** final LoRA with `adapter_config.json` and `adapter_model.safetensors` files.
- **Kaggle Notebook:** validation notebook on `train.csv`.
- **github.com:** source code.

Thank you to the organizers and fellow Kagglers for making this competition a great learning experience!
````

````markdown
## Acknowledgements

First, thank you to NVIDIA and Kaggle for hosting a really fun competition. I entered primarily to gain a deeper understanding of LoRA fine-tuning and training infrastructure, and learned a lot along the way.

My solution builds upon the excellent work by huikang, whose Open Progress Prize Publication laid much of the groundwork.

## Summary

**Code:** <https://github.com/livctr/nvidia-nemotron>

This solution contains three key ingredients: building a workflow that allows for rapid iteration in synthetic prompt and trace generation; staying disciplined with uncovering the data-generation process; and writing clean reasoning traces.

- Complex training schemes did not beat simple cross-entropy loss. I tried focal loss, token loss reweighting, and multi-stage training (with a different data mix and/or learning rate across stages), none of which convincingly beat standard LoRA SFT.
- My biggest gains were in bit manipulation, where my synthetic (generated by code) and LoRA-emitted traces reached 0.9906 and 0.9732 accuracy on `train.csv` respectively.
- I refined the traces in the other categories to ensure the model uses every available signal in the prompt and generates the most-likely guess when the rule is ambiguous.
- I left cryptarithm (which I call "equation transform / symbol") largely untouched.

The table below reports results on `train.csv`. I generate all training data synthetically and use `train.csv` as my validation set. **Public LB: 0.884. Private LB: 0.908.**

| Category | # of Examples | Synthetic trace accuracy | LoRA-emitted trace accuracy |

| Text cipher | 1,576 | 1.0000 | 0.9981 |
| Roman numeral | 1,576 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 |

## Trace generation

The code for this section lives in `nemotron/data/main`, with one pair of files per category: each `_syn.py` generates the synthetic prompts and answers, and each `_cot.py` generates the reasoning trace the model trains on. Feel free to check out the traces as follows:

```bash
# Sample from category: bit_manipulation, physics_gravity, unit_conversion, text_cipher, roman_numeral, equation_transform/numeric, equation_transform/symbol
bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml --inspect --category <category>

# Specific ID
bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml --inspect --id 00457d26
```

### Roman numeral, unit conversion, and physics gravity

Traces here were produced by finding a problem the base model correctly reasons on and converting it into a structured, reproducible format. For unit conversion and physics gravity, care was taken to ensure the dataset's rounding scheme was reproduced exactly; in both, every number in the prompt is rounded to two decimal places.

### Text cipher

The trace builds the mapping that decrypts the letters by looping through the examples, then applies it to the query. The model then guesses the phrase and the sentence template using the 77-word vocabulary and the 4 sentence templates.

What follows is an error-correction loop. The trace iterates each word in the sentence template, and for each word, it finds the corresponding word type (subject, verb, object, location, preposition, adjective) and loops through all words of that word type. I restrict candidates to those within one letter of the decoded length, then score: 1 point for a matching length, 10 per known letter, and 1 per still-missing letter, with the top-scoring word declared as the "true" word.

Overall, the error-correction scheme improved text cipher from $\sim 98.5\%$ to $\sim 99.5\%$, given the same number of training examples. The remaining failure modes were guessing the wrong sentence template or performing the error correction correctly only to substitute the guessed word in the final phrase.

Here is an example of the error correction pipeline on the "verb" word of a "subject verb object" sentence template. The true word is "imagines", scoring 81 points.

```
The second word has role "verb" and has "0 i 1 m 2 a 3 g 4 i 5 n 6 e 7 s 8" 8 letters. But wait, we might be off by one: let's match 7, 8, 9 else no match. So 7 matches, 8 matches, 9 matches. Let's count points. Start with 1 point if the length matches 8 else 0 points. Assign 10 points for matching letters: i, m, a, g, n, e, s. Assign 1 point for missing letters: b, j, k, x, z. Let's track the max for the role "verb".
- chases 6
- creates 7 matches. 0 c 0 r 0 e 10 a 20 t 20 e 30 s 40 => max is 40 for creates.
- discovers 9 matches. 0 d 0 i 10 s 20 c 20 o 20 v 20 e 30 r 30 s 40 => max is 40 for creates.
- draws 5
- dreams 6
- explores 8 matches. 1 e 11 x 12 p 12 l 12 o 12 r 12 e 22 s 32 => max is 40 for creates.
- follows 7 matches. 0 f 0 o 0 l 0 l 0 o 0 w 0 s 10 => max is 40 for creates.
- found 5
- imagines 8 matches. 1 i 11 m 21 a 31 g 41 i 51 n 61 e 71 s 81 => max is 81 for imagines.
- reads 5
- sees 4
- studies 7 matches. 0 s 10 t 10 u 10 d 10 i 20 e 30 s 40 => max is 81 for imagines.
- watches 7 matches. 0 w 0 a 10 t 10 c 10 h 10 e 20 s 30 => max is 81 for imagines.
- writes 6
So max is 81 for imagines. So the true next word by scoring is that exactly: imagines. Thus the next word in phrase is imagines. Thus phrase so far is: cat imagines.
```

### Equation transform / numeric

#### Data generation process

Each problem fixes one domain, normal or reversed, shared by every example, and assigns each of its (typically three) distinct operators a single base arithmetic family — subtraction, addition, multiplication, or concatenation. The base relation is perturbed within its family (+/-1 for addition and multiplication; absolute value and negation for subtraction; modulo, written `max%min`, lives inside the subtraction family) and the chosen domain is applied. The 11 arithmetic rules each appear in a normal and a reversed form (22), and the 2 concatenation rules are domain-independent, for a total of 24 rules. Across the 732 problems, the normal domain accounts for 286 (39.1%) and the reversed domain for the other 446 (60.9%).

| Subtraction | Addition | Multiplication | Concatenation |
|---|---|---|---|
| a-b | a+b | a*b | cat(a,b) -> abcd |
| b-a | a+b+1 | a*b+1 | cat(b,a) -> cdab |
| \|a-b\| | a+b-1 | a*b-1 | |
| -\|a-b\| | | | |
| max%min | | | |

Two other notes:

- For subtraction, a negative result is marked with the operator character before the digits (`opN`) or after (`Nop`), fixed per problem. The placement gates the signed rule: a prefix marker excludes `b-a` and a suffix marker excludes `a-b`, pruning the wrong-direction subtraction.
- Concatenation does not carry the domain. It is its own family with two orderings, `cat(a,b) → abcd` and `cat(b,a) → cdab`, chosen independently per operator. A concatenation operator looks the same whether the problem is normal or reversed, so it never reveals the domain and takes no part in the normal-vs-reversed decision.

#### Procedure

Each distinct operator can be one of 24 rules to start. We iterate through the examples in the problem. The examples eliminate rules that fail to reproduce the output exactly as a string — leading zeros and sign placement included. After this per-example pass, an operator that appears in the examples is typically down to 1-3 candidates.

Attention then turns to the query operator. If it has not been seen, it starts with all 24 rules. We then narrow the candidates:

- **Normal vs. reversed from the other operators.** If the other operators pin the domain and there are only normal or reversed rules remaining, this pins the query operator's domain. Concatenation operators abstain.
- **Normal vs. reversed from zeros in the query.** A leading zero in the query's own operands (e.g. `08`) pins the reversed domain, and a trailing zero (e.g. `50`) pins the normal domain.
- **Base arithmetic family based on the other symbols.** No two operators share the same base relation (subtraction, addition, multiplication). Let the other operators claim their family; assign the query operator to the bucket that is left. If multiple buckets remain, the priority is subtraction, addition, and multiplication. Note that I expected at most three distinct operation symbols in a problem.
- **`a-b` vs `b-a` for subtraction.** The position of the negative-sign marker encodes `a-b` versus `b-a`, pruning the wrong-direction subtraction rule.
- **Base family based on query glyph.** If the query glyph is a literal `+`, `-`, or `*`, survivors are restricted to that family. This rule comes from the observation that `+`, `-`, or `*` are most frequent and normally represent addition, subtraction, or multiplication, respectively.

Whatever survives is committed in a fixed priority order — by domain (normal before reversed, concatenation last), and within a domain by family (subtraction, then addition, then multiplication, each taking the canonical rule before its +/-1 or sign variants) — so the procedure always emits a single best guess rather than abstaining.

### Bit manipulation

My solution builds off directly from huikang's bit manipulation solution, which solves 85% of problems. With reasonable hypotheses about the data generation process, this solution solves 99% of problems.

#### Hypothesized generator

Denote `P` as an atom. Atoms can be one of 21 operations on the input (3 atom types × 7 shift amounts): rotate-left `ROTk` (cyclic, bits wrap), shift-left `SHLk`, and shift-right `SHRk` (both zero-fill), where $k \in 1..7$ ($k \in 1..7$ vs. $k \in 0..7$ is important later). Binary operations between atoms include AND, OR, XOR (e.g. `P1 op P2`) and the negated-second-operand variants ANDNOT, ORNOT, XORNOT (e.g. `P1 op ¬P2`). Denote `OP` as any one of these six binary operations, and let `a` denote the left shift amount, `b` the left rotation amount, and `c` the right shift amount. Every rule belongs to the following grammar:

| Family | Order | Form | Share |
|---|---|---|---|
| no-op | 1 | `P` | 9.1% |
| one-op | 2 | `P1 OP P2` | 51.6% |
| 2-op (Shape A/B) | 3 | `(SHRc OR ¬ROTb) XOR SHLa` or `(SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc` | 18.7% |
| Majority | 3 | `Maj(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb)` | 12.4% |
| Choice | 3 | `Ch(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb) = (SHLa AND SHRc) OR (¬SHLa AND ROTb)` | 4.7% |
| 2-op (Shape C) | 3 | `((SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc) AND ¬(SHLa AND ROTb AND SHRc)` | 3.5% |

In the table above, the order denotes the number of distinct atoms used (an n-op rule applies n binary ops to n+1 atoms, hence order n+1). A rule's signature is its per-bit operator pattern:

| bit | 0 | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SHLa | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 | IN6 | IN7 | | | |
| ROTb | IN1 | IN2 | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 | IN6 | IN7 | IN0 |
| SHRc | | | IN0 | IN1 | IN2 | IN3 | IN4 | IN5 |
| region | L | L | M | M | M | R | R | R |

Each cell shows the input bit `INx` that atom reads (`SHLa[i] = IN(a+i)`, `ROTb[i] = IN((b+i) mod 8)`, `SHRc[i] = IN(i-c)`). An atom is live at a bit when it reads a real input bit, and dead (zero-filled, shown blank) when its shift has run off the end: `SHLa` is dead past bit 7−a, `SHRc` before bit c, while `ROTb` is always live since it wraps. The output thus breaks into contiguous regions. For every family, there are at most 3 regions in the signatures. In general, the number of regions equals the rule's order (here both 3).

For example, `Maj(SHL3, SHR2, ROT1)` has three regions resolving as:

- **Left (bits 0–1):** `SHR2` is dead (zero-filled), so `Maj(SHL3, 0, ROT1) = AND(SHL3, ROT1)` — a 2nd-order AND, written `AND13`.
- **Middle (bits 2–4):** all three atoms are live, so the full 3-input `Maj(SHL3, SHR2, ROT1)`, written `Majority316` (the 6 is from 8-c=8-2=6 since a right shift by c equals a left rotation by 8-c over the non-zero portion).
- **Right (bits 5–7):** `SHL3` is dead, so `Maj(0, SHR2, ROT1) = AND(SHR2, ROT1)` — again a 2nd-order AND, written `AND61`.

It's possible that the number of regions for a rule is less than its order. For example, consider `Maj(SHLa, SHRc, ROTb)` with a = b. For bits 0 through 7-a, `SHLa` equals `ROTa`, and since `Maj(ROTa, SHRc, ROTa) = ROTa`, those bits are the input rotated left by a (which I denote as `Ia`). Bits 8-a to 7 are `Maj(0, SHRc, ROTb)`, which equals the AND between the input shifted right by c and the input rotated left by b (which I denote as `ANDb{8-c}`, again since a right shift by c equals a left rotation by 8-c over the non-zero portion). Hence, this Maj rule leaves a two-region signature.

Importantly, under the data-generation hypothesis, a, b, and c range from 1 to 7. Because every shift is at least 1, `SHRc` is dead at bit 0 and `SHLa` is dead at bit 7, so both left and right regions have at most two live atoms (the always-live `ROTb` plus either shift). Therefore, for every rule in the grammar, the left and right regions (for no-op, these overlap on all 8 bits) are at most 2nd-order functions of the input:

- **0th-order (LOW, HIGH):** the output bit is a constant 0 or 1, reading no input bit.
- **1st-order (Identity, NOT):** the output bit is a single (rotated) input bit, as-is or complemented.
- **2nd-order (AND, OR, XOR, ANDNOT, ORNOT, XORNOT):** the output bit is a boolean function of two (rotated) input bits.

This fact justifies why we only need to consider these 10 functions for the corner regions (the left region that includes bit 0 or the right region that includes bit 7). Further, the corner regions can narrow down the operator pattern for the middle region and determine how long the regions should be: this means we can enumerate left/right region pairs, filter for pairs that fit the signature, and use the left/right pairings to determine the signature. "Final summary E" of this MD file includes a comprehensive list of signatures. The middle region is one of three forms — LOW, NOT, or an "unknown" function. Only the unknown case needs a brute-force check.

#### Trace generation

I'll use ID `66b1c512` as the walk-through example. Feel free to follow along with `bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml --inspect --id 66b1c512`. The rule is the 2-op `(SHL4 XOR ¬ROT7) OR SHR6` with signature `XORNOT47 NOT7 ORNOT27` and lengths `4 2 2`.

First, the trace parses the examples and represents the 8 input and output columns as a hybrid hex-binary "column signature" (not to be confused with the rule's signature). The column signature for bit position i is the "vectorized" representation of the input/output values at bit position i for the 7-10 examples. With 10 examples, that gives 2 hex digits and 2 binary digits. Hex letters A-F get a leading space so they do not merge with other letters, and a space separates the hex and binary portions. Second, still following huikang's bit manipulation solution, the trace tries matching functions of the input columns (LOW, HIGH, Identity, NOT, AND, OR, XOR, ANDNOT, ORNOT, XORNOT) with the output columns. The `47│1 B 00 match 0` line below shows that the XORNOT of input columns 4 and 7 matches output column 0. The lines under XORNOT output matches aggregate these matches by output column, dropping the column signatures.

Then, we walk inwards from the left and right sides. Each line represents a chain, and we start a chain based on the output column matches at bits 0 (for left) and 7 (for right). An `x` represents where the run breaks. Departing from huikang's bit manipulation solution, we store shifts rather than columns, so each chain resolves to a shift-tagged operator such as `XORNOT47`. `XORNOT47` means bit i of the output equals the XORNOT of input bits `(i+4)%8` and `(i+7)%8`.

In the example below, the line `0 47│1 50│2 61│3 72│4 03x XORNOT47 length 4 1` reads: XORNOT of input columns 4 and 7 matches output bit 0, and walking inward each column steps up by one — 5,0 at bit 1, 6,1 at bit 2, 7,2 at bit 3 — until it breaks at bit 4 (`4 03x`). In other words, bits 0-3 can be explained by `XORNOT47` (left region). Similarly, bits 6-7 can be explained by `ORNOT27` (right region). Only bits 4-5 remain to be explained (middle region).

There are 4 additional implementation details:

- The trace only tests 8C2=28 input column combinations for symmetric ops (AND, OR, XOR, XORNOT), rather than all 8*7=56 combinations for asymmetric ops (ANDNOT, ORNOT).
- We test middle bits for LOW and NOT since many 3-region signatures have those as their middle region. The block below shows what middle-bit matching for NOT looks like. Here, `NOT745` means NOT with shift 7, starting from bit 4 and ending on bit 5.
- The two numbers after "length" are the chain's run length and a running counter of same-length chains seen so far in this block. The running counter helps the model enumerate the shift-tagged operators.
- After "Best nonzero" come the best length, the number of chains tied at it, and each best operator prefixed with its index. Because $k \in 1..7$, we list only nonzero-shift operators to avoid spurious matches.

After enumerating through the possible functions, we summarize the longest run in each function family as follows:

```

After summarizing the runs, we determine which candidate signatures to enumerate. As was conjectured by the data-generation hypothesis, every signature in the table falls into one of four cases by region count (the specific signatures are located in `bit_manipulation_bit_formulas.md`):

- **One region (no-op):** the whole output is one operator: `Ib` (rotation), HIGH, or `ANDab` (a Maj collapsed to one Ix AND Iy).
- **Two region (one-op, or merged-twin multi-op):** Left + Right, no live middle — a one-op rule, or a multi-op whose two corners are the same op on a shared digit (e.g. `ANDab`/`ANDbc`).
- **Three region, middle LOW or middle NOT:** Left + Right + a constant/negation filler. This case occurs when the dead part of SHL and SHR overlap.
- **Three region, UNKNOWN middle:** the middle is 2nd-order or higher (Majority, Choice, a 2-op (Shape A/B), or XOR-shift). This case occurs when SHL and SHR have no overlapping dead part (e.g. when both a and c are small).

One region (no-op) and three region, live/UNKNOWN middle always run. The line `Left longest 4 right longest 2 sum longest 6 so skip` determines whether two region runs (here, we skip). The line `Middle fillers span and are NOT745 so test each` determines whether three region runs (here, we test NOT745).

```
Test no middle if sum longest is at least 8
Left longest 4 right longest 2 sum longest 6 so skip
Left longest covers 0 1 2 3
Right longest covers 7 6
Middle remaining is 4 5
Middle either spans remaining or not
NOT745 shift 7 covers 4 to 5 spans
Middle fillers span and are NOT745 so test each
```

We then enumerate the regions and the signatures in each region. The next block demonstrates Three region, middle NOT. Scanning through the lines, we're testing the middle `NOT745` with shift 7, left threshold 4, and total threshold 6. Each family pair tests a pairing of corner regions. A family pair is "long" if the longest length in the left family meets the left threshold and the longest lengths in the left and right families sum to meet the total threshold. These length guards ensure the runs are long enough to cover the bits.

If a family pair is "long", we display every shift-tagged operator in the left family that matches the shift (here "7" from `NOT745`; every other region enumeration has no such shift requirement), each taking a line. On each line, we display every shift-tagged operator in the right family that matches the left family's shift. The left, middle, and right should share the same shift because they share the shift b from rotation, which is used at all bit positions (the exception is Identity/Identity for the XOR rule).

| Class | Members | Match rule |
|---|---|---|
| Symmetric | Identity, NOT, AND, OR, XOR, XORNOT | either operand may be b |
| Constant | LOW, HIGH | no operand, always matches |
| Asymmetric | ANDNOT, ORNOT | if left family, first digit is b; if right family, second digit is b |

After pair-matching, we emit the "Options are" block. In this example,

- `XORNOT47 ORNOT27 NOT745 lengths 4 2 2` shows the candidate in Left-Right-Middle order with their observed run lengths. Here left, middle, and right regions share shift b = 7; `XORNOT47`'s other digit gives a = 4, and `ORNOT27`'s gives 8 − c = 2 (so c = 6).
- Certain family pairs have requirements on `a - (8 - c)` (needs to be positive, zero, or negative). Here, this pair passes: `needs positive 4-2=2 pass`.
- True lengths can be derived from the shifts: `true lengths min(8-4,8-2)=4 min(4,2)=2 2`.
- Multiple pairs may reach this stage. A candidate's predicted (true) corner lengths should match the lengths the walk observed, so we score each by its length error — `|true − observed left length| + |true − observed right length|` — and take the smallest. Here `|4-4|+|2-2|=0 best` has a length error of 0, which is unbeatable. We take the first candidate to achieve the smallest length error (assuming all other checks pass) as the predicted signature.

HIGH absent ORNOT second digit 2
XORNOT 4 long HIGH absent
Identity absent Identity absent special exception ignore digits
Identity absent AND absent
AND absent Identity absent
ANDNOT first digit absent Identity absent
AND first digit absent AND both digits absent
AND second digit absent AND both digits absent
XORNOT 4 long ORNOT second digit 2 6 long

Options are
 XORNOT47 ORNOT27 NOT745 lengths 4 2 2│ needs positive 4-2=2 pass true lengths min(8-4,8-2)=4 min(4,2)=2 2 |4-4|+|2-2|=0 best
```

The final answer is: 11000010
```

When the middle is live (not this example), we predict the middle-region form from the family pair and verify bit-by-bit. For example, AND/AND indicates Majority, ANDNOT/Identity indicates Choice, Identity/Identity indicates XOR.

The block below shows ID `00890aff` with rule `Maj(SHL2, SHR1, ROT6)`: the AND/AND corners `AND26`/`AND67` (shared b = 6) predict the middle `Majority267`, verified against every example.

```
Left right middle unknown with left threshold 1 and total threshold 2 and pass if overlap negative
...
AND first digit 1 long AND both digits 2 3 long
 AND61│ AND67
 AND26│ none
AND second digit 1 long AND both digits 2 3 long
 AND61│ none
 AND26│ AND67
Best absolute sum so far is none so test passed options on input and output bit columns immediately for absolute sum 0 and later for 1 and higher until match
Options are
 AND61 AND67 Majority167 lengths 1 2 6│1-7=-6 pass true lengths min(8-1,8-7)=1 min(1,7)=1 6 |1-1|+|1-2|=1 test
 AND26 AND67 Majority267 lengths 1 2 5│2-7=-5 pass true lengths min(8-2,8-7)=1 min(2,7)=2 5 |1-1|+|2-2|=0 test
1│Majority267 = Majority(IN3, IN7, IN0) = Majority(1001 1100 11, 0011 1110 10, 0100 0010 10) = 0001 1110 10 match match match
2│Majority267 = Majority(IN4, IN0, IN1) = Majority(0111 0111 11, 0100 0010 10, 1100 1111 01) = 0100 0111 11 match match match
3│Majority267 = Majority(IN5, IN1, IN2) = Majority(0001 1001 01, 1100 1111 01, 1101 0101 11) = 1101 1101 01 match match match
4│Majority267 = Majority(IN6, IN2, IN3) = Majority(0110 0001 01, 1101 0101 11, 1001 1100 11) = 1101 0101 11 match match match
5│Majority267 = Majority(IN7, IN3, IN4) = Majority(0011 1110 10, 1001 1100 11, 0111 0111 11) = 0011 1110 11 match match match
```

Because all middle bits match for `Majority267`, that becomes our middle. Choice is handled similarly, but because c never shows at the corners, the trace sweeps c = 1..7 (e.g. ID `000b53cf`). Up to now, every family except for 2-op (Shape C) is handled.

Finally, we do two fallbacks, which are run when no candidate has a length error below 4:

- **Over-run.** We may have a spurious match longer than the true match in a op family. We search the runs within the families until the first hit with length error 0 (e.g. ID `649bebaf`).
- **Shape C.** If no shorter corner fits, take the longest XORNOT/ORNOT pair and evaluate Shape C, `((SHLa XOR ¬ROTb) OR SHRc) AND ¬(SHLa AND ROTb AND SHRc)` (e.g. ID `05b5ffe1`).

The last 1% of rows have more than one signature fitting the 7-10 examples, making prediction ambiguous. We order the testing of signatures such that the first candidate to achieve the smallest length error has lower order (e.g. ID `82d937aa`).

Overall, this solution:

- Keeps in mind the 7680-token budget: employs hex-binary, avoids double computation for commutative binary ops, enumerates two-region and three-region with middle LOW or middle NOT only when necessary, and minimizes per-bit brute-force verification by stopping at the first full match.
- Reduces spurious matches by considering nonzero-shift operators only and matching based on signatures.
- Uses shift logic to determine the middle bits and true region lengths.

### Equation transform / symbol

I largely left this category alone. For $n$ distinct digits, a brute-force solver would have to enumerate $n!$ symbol-to-digit mappings. Assuming each `ab [op] cd = x` takes at least 7 tokens, that gives a testing budget of 1100 combinations, which means we can only enumerate over 6 distinct symbols at most (6! = 720, 7! = 5040, only two problems of 823 have <=6 distinct symbols). Other top teams used a "signature-based" prediction idea similar to the one I used for bit manipulation: the form of `ab [op] cd = x` tells you which symbol-digit mappings to enumerate, reducing the search space.

My solution follows the idea by huikang in the Open Progress Prize Publication. It handles concatenation and reversed concatenation. Touch-ups include:

- Guessing the first symbol seen when it is clear the query operator is neither concatenation nor reversed concatenation.
- Refining the trace to look more similar to my solution for equation transform / numeric.
- Using the non-ASCII delimiter `│` and the Nemotron tokenizer to make parsing easier to understand for the Nemotron model. This is the reason behind the strange spacing and newlines in the below trace. I found that this helped roughly 5-10 examples of the 823 total examples.
- To deal with `}` symbols, I emit in the format `The final answer is: <answer>` rather than `\boxed{<answer>}`. This format is replicated to the other categories for consistency.

One example is parsed as follows:

```
Example 1
*[-$( = *[$(
The target is *[$(
= │ *[$(
│ = │ *││[$││(
│ = │ *││[││$││(
│ = │*││[││$││(│
- concatenation? │*[-$(│ = │*││[-││$(│ = │*││[││-││$││(│ = │*││[││$││(│ = │ *││[││$││(│ = │ *││[$││(│ = │ *[$(│ = *[$( = │ *││[$││(│ = │ *││[││$││(│ = │*││[││$││(│
- target │*││[││$││(│ and concatenation │*││[││$││(│ match? Yes.
- concatenation reversed? │*[-$(│ reversed = │*││[-││$(│ reversed = │*││[││-││$││(│ reversed = │*││[││$││(│ reversed = │$││(││*││[│ = │ $││(││*││[│ = │ $(││*││[│ = │ $(*[│ = $(*[ = │ $(││*││[│ = │ $││(││*││[│ = │$││(││*││[│
- target │*││[││$││(│ and concatenation reversed │$││(││*││[│ match? No.
So what is the operator? │*││[││-││$││(│ has operator │-│. Is │-│ concatenation, concatenation reversed, or unknown? Probably concatenation.
```

## Modeling and workflow

### Workflow

- Make edits under `nemotron/data/main/` in my repo and create/edit a configuration file under `configs/`.
- Generate data via `bash generate_traces.sh --config configs/final.yaml`.
- Train the model and auto-submit to my Kaggle notebook for validation: `bash train_sft.sh --config configs/final.yaml --backend [mbridge|tinker] --experiment my_experiment`.
- Analyze results with `bash analyze_adapter.sh --pull-kaggle`.

To figure out my hypotheses for the data generation process, I would ask Claude questions and have it write scripts under `scripts/discovery`. Claude wrote the orchestration in my code and wrote 95% of the data generation code, with some formatting changes made by me.

To save training tokens during the experimental process, I noticed that I could focus on one domain at a time. For example, I could train and validate just on text cipher. This was very useful before coming to bit manipulation since the other categories required far fewer tokens to train.

### Tinker vs Megatron-Bridge training infrastructure

My early experiments ran on Tinker, but switching to Megatron-Bridge turned out to matter a lot: in one run, changing nothing but the backend raised bit manipulation accuracy from 0.81 to 0.89 (against a synthetic-trace ceiling of 0.91 for the category at the time). The reason is that a Tinker LoRA requires a lossy SVD to be converted into the PEFT format, whereas a Megatron-Bridge LoRA maps to PEFT exactly.

Late in the competition, I discovered a bug in my code that converts the Megatron-Core distributed checkpoint into a HF PEFT adapter. I caught it late because my internal validation scores stayed high despite it, and fixing it made little difference: public LB went 0.884 -> 0.880 and private LB stayed 0.908. Megatron stores a fused QKV projection for the attention layers, and my extractor split the B LoRA matrix into separate q/k/v with a plain contiguous slice, whereas Megatron interleaves Q/K/V per query group. The bug thus mixed up Q, K, and V rows. I find it strange that my internal validation was still so high even with this bug. I can only hypothesize that most of the adaptation lives in other layers, especially the MoE layers.

### Final training details

| Parameter | Value | Note |
|---|---|---|
| num_epochs | 1 | |
| learning_rate → min_learning_rate | 2e-4 → 1e-5 | cosine, no warmup |
| seq_length | 8192 | packing always on |
| micro_batch_size | 1 | required with packing |
| global_batch_size | 12 | in packs; also the stratify window |
| expert_model_parallel_size | 4 | EP=4 — only 32 distinct expert adapters, tiled across the 128 experts (see note) |
| moe_token_dispatcher_type | alltoall | A100; flex+deepep is H100-only |
| moe_grouped_gemm | false | per-expert LoRA (~888M trainable) vs shared (~37M) |
| moe_layer_recompute | true | frees expert activations so the Mamba backward fits ~80GB |
| peft_dim / peft_alpha / peft_dropout | 32 / 32 / 0.05 | |
| peft_target_modules | linear_qkv, linear_proj, linear_fc1, linear_fc2, in_proj, out_proj, output_layer | attention, Mamba in/out proj, MoE FC, LM head |
| eval_iters / eval_per_epoch | 32 / true | eval each epoch boundary |
| dtype | bfloat16 | |
| training examples | 57,600 | bit_manip 10,800 · text_cipher 10,800 · eq_numeric 9,000 · eq_symbol 9,000 · physics 6,000 · unit 6,000 · roman 6,000 |
| training tokens | 159,336,343 | all synthetic; 1 epoch |
| hardware | 4× A100 (80GB) | |
| throughput | ~15M tokens/hr | |
| wall-clock | 11 hr train, 4 hr validate on Kaggle | |

Notes:

- Validation results were generally quite robust to the learning rate (between 1e-4 and 3e-4).
- `moe_grouped_gemm: false` attaches a per-expert LoRA.
- `expert_model_parallel_size: 4` with 4 GPUs shards the base model's 128 experts across them (32 per GPU), cutting per-GPU memory enough to fit the 8192-token sequence length. I did not realize at the time that this layout tiles the LoRA weights across the sharded experts: only 32 distinct A/B matrices are learned for the 128 experts, cutting LoRA capacity ~4x (≈880M → ≈220M free parameters). I don't think this had a large impact on the final results — the synthetic vs. LoRA-emitted traces differ by only $0.3\%$ accuracy.
- There are large diminishing returns after around 80M tokens. I believe it would have been possible to place second in this competition with a LoRA trained on 80M tokens. Designing accurate and learnable traces was more important (and also more human-intensive).
- Training `output_layer` is extremely important, especially if you want to include tokens in the long-tailed end of the vocabulary (e.g. the non-ASCII `│` separator).

## Conclusion

My key ingredient in this competition is synthetic data generation. As huikang mentions, it helps to think of the adapter as a computer. This computer manages:

- **Storage:** facts the weights can memorize during training (e.g. the bit manipulation signatures, text cipher words).
- **Compute:** each reasoning step should use inputs that are already explicitly in the trace. The smaller the positional distance between an input and the step that consumes it, the better.

- **Kaggle Notebook:** validation notebook on `train.csv`.
````

## PART 1 — The two loop skills `dev-plan` and `dev-loop`

Both are Claude Code skills under `.claude/skills/`. They are a **matched pair**: `dev-plan` produces the plan/spec (and optionally an implementation-readiness handoff); `dev-loop` consumes that handoff to implement. Both use an **autonomous, read-only Codex CLI reviewer** (`gpt-5.5`, `reasoning_effort=xhigh`) where **Claude writes/fixes and Codex only audits** — Codex emits `audit.json`, and the orchestrator (Claude) publishes the audit comment on its behalf.

### `dev-plan` (`.claude/skills/dev-plan/SKILL.md`)
- **Purpose:** turn a feature request source into a reviewed planning/spec PR with registered epics/stories, a tracking issue, and a bounded external review loop.
- **Invocation:** `/dev-plan &lt;issue:N|pr:N|N|path-to-spec-or-zip&gt; [mode=impl]` (`disable-model-invocation: true` — slash/explicit only). First arg mandatory; bare number resolves PR-first-then-issue.
- **Inputs:** a GitHub issue, PR, plain spec file, or `.zip` request pack; repo planning conventions (`CLAUDE.md`, `docs/plan/README.md`, `docs/stories/README.md`, `docs/context/index.md`); live registries.
- **Outputs / artifacts:**
  - Epic docs `docs/plan/wos_&lt;n&gt;_&lt;slug&gt;.md`, story docs `docs/stories/wos_&lt;n&gt;_&lt;slug&gt;.md`, updated plan/story READMEs, OD/ADR entries.
  - One planning/spec PR; at-most-one tracking issue per epic.
  - `mode=impl` only: per-story `docs/stories/&lt;slug&gt;.readiness.json` (conforms to `docs/harness/schemas/implementation-readiness.schema.json`) + epic side-product `docs/stories/&lt;epic-slug&gt;_work_advice.md`.
  - Interview scratch `temp/&lt;yyyyMMdd&gt;_&lt;slug&gt;_spec_&lt;lang&gt;.md` (gitignored, default `zh`); committed docs in `en`.
  - Runtime state `.dev-plan/state/&lt;source&gt;.json`; per-run artifacts `.dev-plan/artifacts/&lt;run_id&gt;/` (`latest` symlink).
- **End-to-end steps:** resolve source → find optional dashboard → collect context → triage scope (exit early for small/complete/non-feature) → gap analysis → interview (decision table, one/small batches) → draft/refine epic+stories → `[mode=impl: Step 7b readiness pass — DoR gate → READY_FOR_IMPL or stays DOC_ONLY]` → open/update tracking issue → open/update ONE planning PR → **Codex review loop** (post audit before fixing, append per round) → fix/rebut (`fix-disposition.json`) → closeout at `READY_FOR_MERGE` (human-merge default).
- **State machine:** `DISCOVER_SOURCE → TRIAGE_SCOPE → COLLECT_CONTEXT → ANALYZE_GAPS → INTERVIEWING → SPEC_LOCKED → DRAFT_PLAN_DOCS → [IMPL_READINESS] → OPEN_OR_UPDATE_SPEC_PR → SYNC_TRACKING_ISSUE → REVIEWING ⇄ FIXING_OR_REBUTTING → READY_FOR_MERGE | WAITING_FOR_HUMAN | SPEC_REWORK → DONE | EXITED`.
- **Two finish lines:** default = `READY_FOR_MERGE` of `DOC_ONLY` design-freezes; `mode=impl` carries finalized stories to `READY_FOR_IMPL` (the contract `/dev-loop` consumes — solves the handoff gap in issue #178).
- **Dependencies:** Codex CLI (or GitHub Action / OpenAI Responses API / manual) reviewer backend; the dev-loop skill downstream; optional Playwright MCP (off by default); optional read-only DB (`SUPABASE_DB_URL`→`SUPABASE_DB_URL2`).
- **Config knobs:** `.dev-plan.yaml` (falls back to `CONFIG.example.yaml`). Key `${WOS_PLAN_*}` overrides: `max_review_turns` (5), `max_question_batch` (5), `base_branch` (main), `allow_auto_merge` (false), `allow_db_read` (true), `interview_language` (zh), `reviewer.model` (gpt-5.5), `reviewer.effort` (xhigh), `approval` (never), `sandbox` (read-only). Structural keys (`docs.*`, patterns, markers) are fixed.

**`dev-plan/CONFIG.example.yaml`** — full documented default config: `schema_version 1.0`; blocks `loop`, `state` (gitignored `.dev-plan/`), `branches` (base main, human-merge default, branch patterns `feat/{feature_abbr}-wos-{epic_number}`, `temp/{owner_or_agent}/{slug}`), `source_resolution`, `docs`, `tracking` (dashboard search by title keywords "Delivery Plan Dashboard"/"kanban" + labels `delivery-plan`/`planning`), `planning` (incl. `impl_readiness` DoR rows: code_deliverables, testable_acceptance_criteria, definition_of_done, validation_commands, zero_open_decisions, buildable_status), `reviewer` (codex-cli, `codex_github_action` disabled, `pro_audit` gpt-5.5-pro disabled), `security` (db_env_vars, `env_files: [.vscode/.env]`, forbidden_outputs), `github` (round-specific audit markers), `human_gate`, `merge`, `validation` (npm run docs:check / inventory:audit / inventory:map / ci:local).

**`dev-plan/schemas/`** — `audit.schema.json` (dev-plan external audit output), `decision.schema.json` (OD-*/ADR-* ledger), `fix-disposition.schema.json` (fix/rebut disposition).

**`dev-plan/scripts/`** — `resolve-source.sh` (resolve arg to one source), `find-plan-dashboard.sh` (locate optional dashboard issue), `collect-context.sh` (gather planning context), `validate-plan-docs.sh` (registry structural checks), `render-tracking-issue.py`, `render-pr-body.py`, `render-codex-command.py` (render Codex cmd, no exec), `run-codex-review.sh` (run autonomous read-only review), `classify-audit.py` (audit.json → routing token), `render-readiness.py` (emit + DoR-gate readiness artifact), `resolve_config.py` (load `.dev-plan.yaml` w/ `${VAR:default}` expansion), `scan_secrets.py` (single secret-safety gate), `publish-status-comment.sh` (post status/round PR comment).

**`dev-plan/templates/`** — `interview_spec_en.md` / `interview_spec_zh.md` (interview decision tables), `implementation_scope.md` (readiness scope), `tracking_issue.md`, `planning_pr_body.md`, `codex_review_prompt.md`, `claude_fix_prompt.md`, `audit_comment.md` (marker `&lt;!-- dev-plan-audit r{round} --&gt;`), `closeout_comment.md`, `work_advice.md`.

### `dev-loop` (`.claude/skills/dev-loop/SKILL.md`)
- **Purpose:** drive a locked target through implementation → local validation → PR → autonomous Codex review → fix/rebut → fresh review → merge readiness. Implementation only, not planning.
- **Invocation:** `/dev-loop &lt;issue:N|pr:N|N|WOS-epic|WOS-story[,...]|path-to-task-file&gt;` (also `disable-model-invocation: true`). Resumable from `.dev-loop/state/&lt;slug&gt;.json`, PR, issue, branch, prior artifacts.
- **Inputs:** the target + `.dev-loop.yaml` (single source of truth). **Prefers the dev-plan handoff** `docs/stories/&lt;slug&gt;.readiness.json`; if a story is `DOC_ONLY` / has no readiness artifact it **stops and recommends `/dev-plan &lt;target&gt; mode=impl`**.
- **Outputs / artifacts:** code + tests; the PR (body from `templates/pr_body.md`); `validation.json`, `audit.json`, `fix-disposition.json`, `browser-evidence.json` under `.dev-loop/artifacts/pr-&lt;pr&gt;/r&lt;round&gt;/`; state `.dev-loop/state/&lt;slug&gt;.json`; PR audit + fix-disposition comments (round-specific markers, append never overwrite); tracking-issue/dashboard sync.
- **State machine:** `TARGET_RESOLVED → SCOPE_VALIDATED → IMPLEMENTING → LOCAL_VALIDATION → PR_OPENED → READY_FOR_EXTERNAL_REVIEW → EXTERNAL_REVIEW_RUNNING → FIXING_OR_REBUTTING → FIX_VALIDATION → READY_FOR_HUMAN_MERGE → MERGED` (↘ `WAITING_FOR_HUMAN` / `BLOCKED`). Every review/fix bound to exact `head_sha`; HEAD change ⇒ stale evidence.
- **Steps:** resolve target → find dashboard → collect context → reject/redirect unsuitable work → classify work-kind → **lock scope** (`validate-scope.py`, exit 20/21 ⇒ redirect `/dev-plan`) → implement (drive locked scope as a `/goal`) → local validation → request Codex review (`codex exec --ask-for-approval never --sandbox workspace-write --output-schema … --output-last-message …`) → classify audit → fix/rebut/defer → loop to `max_review_turns` → merge readiness (human-merge default) → stop conditions → final report.
- **Reviewer difference vs dev-plan:** dev-loop Codex runs `sandbox=workspace-write` + `network_access=true` (so it can run `gh`/DB/browser evidence and write `audit.json`), but `repo_write_policy=forbidden` and `enforce_no_diff_after_review=true` reverts/invalidates any audit that leaves a worktree change. `danger-full-access` refused either way; reviewer never commits/pushes/comments.
- **Config knobs:** `.dev-loop.yaml` with `${WOS_DEVLOOP_*}` overrides (see Part 2).

**`dev-loop/schemas/`** — `audit.schema.json` (Codex review round output, one per pr/round/head_sha), `fix-disposition.schema.json` (Claude's per-finding disposition), `loop-state.schema.json` (resumable state at `.dev-loop/state/&lt;slug&gt;.json`), `review-target.schema.json` (resolved target).

**`dev-loop/scripts/`** — `resolve-target.sh`, `find-plan-dashboard.sh`, `collect-context.sh`, `classify-work-kind.py`, `validate-scope.py` (scope-complete + zero-open-decisions gate), `run-local-validation.sh`, `run-codex-review.sh` (enforces no-diff + HEAD), `classify-audit.py`, `render-audit-comment.py`, `publish-pr-comment.sh`, `sync-tracking-issue.sh`, `sync-plan-dashboard.sh` (delegates to repo `scripts/plan/sync-dashboard.mjs`), `browser-evidence.sh` (Playwright-MCP UI evidence), `verify-head-sha.sh` (stale check, exit 3), `resolve_config.py`, `lib/config.sh`.

**`dev-loop/templates/`** — `pr_body.md`, `codex_review_prompt.md`, `claude_fix_prompt.md`, `audit_comment.md`, `fix_disposition_comment.md`, `review_request.md`, `tracking_issue_update.md`, `closeout_comment.md`.
